en.learnText: New to Sudoku, or stuck on a hard puzzle? Two guides explain the rules and every solving technique the hints use, each with a real example.

labels.hint: In the game, the hint says: {text}
labels.legend: Bold digits are given, blue digits were placed while solving, small digits are candidates. Highlighted cells form the pattern, crossed-out candidates are removed, and a circled candidate is the digit to place.
labels.notation: Cells are written as r3c7: row 3, column 7. Rows are counted from the top, columns from the left, and boxes 1 to 9 from the top left, row by row.

howTo.title: How to Play Sudoku: Rules, Board and First Moves
howTo.description: Learn how to play Sudoku: the rules, how rows, columns and boxes work, why every puzzle has one solution, how to use notes and how to make your first moves.
howTo.summary: Sudoku is a logic puzzle on a 9×9 grid. Fill every empty cell with a digit from 1 to 9 so that each row, each column and each 3×3 box contains every digit exactly once. Some digits are given at the start; you deduce the rest, one certain cell at a time, and you never have to guess. This guide explains the board, the rules, the single-solution principle, notes and a simple strategy for your first moves. You can practise everything in [Bare Sudoku](play), which is free and has hints that explain the logic.

sections.h: What are the rules of Sudoku?
p: There are only three rules, and they are the same rule seen from three directions: every row must contain the digits 1 to 9, every column must contain the digits 1 to 9, and every 3×3 box must contain the digits 1 to 9. A digit can therefore never appear twice in the same row, column or box.

The given digits, printed in bold, are fixed. Your job is to fill the empty cells. There is no arithmetic and no ordering: the digits are just nine different symbols. You could play with letters or shapes and nothing would change.

The board has 81 cells in 9 rows and 9 columns. Thick lines divide it into nine 3×3 boxes. Each cell belongs to exactly one row, one column and one box, and these three groups are its units. The 20 other cells that share a unit with a cell are called its peers; a digit placed in a cell rules that digit out in all 20 peers.

Cells are written as r3c7: row 3, column 7. Rows are counted from the top, columns from the left, and boxes 1 to 9 from the top left, row by row. This notation is used in every technique guide and is worth learning: r5c5 is the centre of the board.

sections.h: Why does every Sudoku have exactly one solution?
p: A proper Sudoku has one solution, and that is what makes logic work. Whenever you can show that a digit cannot go anywhere else in a unit, it must go in the remaining cell, because the solution exists and is unique. If a puzzle had two solutions, no amount of reasoning could tell them apart and you would be forced to guess at some point.

Bare Sudoku generates every puzzle on your device and checks that it has exactly one solution and that its logical solver can finish it with the techniques of the chosen level. So if you are stuck, there is always a next step to find, and the hint shows it.

sections.h: How do you start a Sudoku puzzle?
p: Start with what is most constrained. This order works at every level:
list: Pick a digit that already appears many times, say six or seven, and find the boxes that still miss it. Often only one cell in a box is left for it: that is a [hidden single](hidden-single).

Look for crowded cells. A cell whose row, column and box together contain eight different digits has only one candidate left: a [naked single](naked-single). Cells in nearly full rows or boxes are the best place to look.
Every digit you place removes a candidate from 20 peers, so check those peers straight away. Singles tend to come in chains.

When the easy placements dry up, write notes: the candidates for each empty cell. Then look for a digit that is confined to one line inside a box ([locked candidates](locked-candidates)) or two cells that share the same two candidates (a [naked pair](naked-pairs)).
Return to singles after every elimination. Even Expert puzzles are solved mostly by singles; the advanced technique just unlocks the next one.

sections.h: What are notes and when should you use them?
p: Notes, also called pencil marks or candidates, are the small digits you write in an empty cell to record which digits are still possible there. In easy puzzles you rarely need them; from Hard upward they are essential, because techniques like pairs, X-Wing and Y-Wing are about candidates, not placed digits.

Keep notes accurate: when you place a digit, remove it from the notes of all 20 peers. In Bare Sudoku this happens automatically, and Fill notes writes every candidate into every empty cell with one tap, so you can start from a complete, correct set of candidates. A note is a fact, not a guess: it means that nothing rules this digit out yet.

sections.h: What should you do when you are stuck?
p: First recheck the basics: every nearly full row, column and box is a source of singles. Then make sure the notes are complete, because a missing candidate hides patterns and a stale one creates false ones. Then work through the [techniques](techniques) in order of difficulty: locked candidates, pairs and triples, then advanced patterns such as X-Wing, Y-Wing and the Skyscraper. Each has its own page with a real example.

If nothing works, take a hint. In Bare Sudoku the hint first checks whether a placed digit is wrong, then finds the next cell that can be filled by logic and names the technique, so you learn something even when you use it. Tap the hint again to place the digit.

sections.h: How do you enter digits in Bare Sudoku?
p: Tap a cell, then a digit. Or tap a digit first: it locks, and every cell you tap receives it, which is the fastest way to place the sixth, seventh and eighth copy of a digit. Tap the digit again to release it. The Notes button switches to pencil marks, Erase clears a cell, Undo takes back any move, and mistakes are marked in red unless you turn that off in the menu.

On a keyboard, use the arrow keys to move, 1 to 9 to enter a digit, Backspace to erase, N for notes, U for undo, H for a hint, F to fill notes and Escape for the menu. The game saves itself, works offline and has no ads and no account.

faq: Do you ever need to guess in Sudoku?

Not in a proper puzzle. Every Bare Sudoku puzzle has exactly one solution and is checked to be solvable by logic alone, up to the techniques of its level. If you feel you must guess, a candidate is missing from your notes or a technique is waiting to be found.
Can a digit appear twice in a row, column or box?
No. That is the whole rule: each of the nine rows, nine columns and nine boxes contains every digit from 1 to 9 exactly once. If two identical digits share a unit, at least one of them is wrong.
What is the difference between Easy, Medium, Hard, Expert and Master?

The level is set by the techniques the puzzle needs. Easy and Medium are solved with singles only, and Easy starts with at least 38 given digits. Hard needs locked candidates or pairs and triples. Expert needs at least one advanced pattern, such as an X-Wing, a Y-Wing, a Skyscraper or a Unique Rectangle. Master needs chains, almost locked sets or forcing nets. The number next to the level name is the puzzle's difficulty rating, set by the hardest step it needs.
Is it better to fill notes for every cell or only for some?

For Hard and Expert puzzles, fill them all: patterns such as pairs, X-Wing and Y-Wing only show up when every candidate is written. In Easy and Medium, notes are optional and most players just scan for singles.
How long does a Sudoku take?

An Easy puzzle takes a few minutes; Expert puzzles can take twenty minutes or more, depending on how quickly you spot the advanced pattern. Bare Sudoku shows a timer, pauses it while the menu is open and keeps no leaderboard, so play at your own pace.
Does Sudoku need arithmetic?
No. The digits are only labels; no adding or counting is involved. Any nine symbols would work, and that is why Sudoku is a logic puzzle rather than a number puzzle.

index.title: Sudoku Solving Techniques Explained with Examples
index.description: Sudoku solving techniques from naked singles to X-Wing, Skyscraper and Unique Rectangle, in the order the Bare Sudoku hints use them, each with a real example.
intro: Every Sudoku can be solved with a small set of logical techniques. This index lists the techniques that the Bare Sudoku solver and its hints use, in the order the solver tries them: singles first, then eliminations within one unit, then patterns that span several rows, columns and boxes, including patterns that rely on the puzzle having exactly one solution. Each technique has its own page with a definition, how to spot it, a real example from a generated puzzle and the common mistakes.

The level of a puzzle is decided by the hardest technique it needs. Easy and Medium puzzles need only singles, Hard puzzles need locked candidates or pairs and triples, Expert puzzles need at least one advanced pattern, such as a fish, a wing, a Skyscraper or a Unique Rectangle, and Master puzzles need chains or other techniques beyond this guide. Whatever the level, singles do most of the work; the advanced technique removes a candidate or two and singles carry on from there.
faq: In which order should I try Sudoku techniques?

Cheapest first, in the order of this index: singles, then locked candidates, then naked and hidden pairs and triples, then the advanced patterns, starting with X-Wing. Bare Sudoku tries its techniques in exactly this order and always applies the first one that makes progress; a hint names the hardest technique it needed to reach the next digit.
Do I need all these techniques to solve Sudoku?

For Easy and Medium puzzles, singles are enough. Hard puzzles add locked candidates and subsets. Expert puzzles need at least one advanced pattern, such as a fish, a wing, a Skyscraper or a Unique Rectangle, but usually only once or twice per puzzle. Master puzzles go further and need chains or other techniques that this guide does not cover.
Are there harder techniques than the ones in this guide?

Yes. Players have described many more techniques for the hardest puzzles, and new ones keep appearing. Bare Sudoku uses several of them beyond the pages here: more fish, wings and rectangle patterns at Expert level, and chains, almost locked sets and forcing nets at Master level. The hint always names the technique it used, so you can look it up even when this guide has no page for it yet.
What is a candidate?

A digit that could still go in an empty cell because nothing in its row, column or box rules it out yet. Notes in the game are candidates. Every technique beyond singles reasons about candidates, so keep them complete and accurate.

naked-single.name: Naked single
naked-single.title: Naked Single in Sudoku: The Cell with One Candidate
naked-single.description: A naked single is an empty cell with only one possible digit. Learn how to find naked singles quickly, with a real example step by step and the usual mistakes.
naked-single.summary: A naked single is an empty cell that has exactly one candidate: the other eight digits already appear in its row, column or box. The remaining digit must go there. It is the simplest Sudoku technique, the one you use most, and the one the Bare Sudoku hint reports as "Only one candidate here".
when: Always. Naked singles appear from the first move to the last, at every level. In Easy and Medium puzzles they are, together with hidden singles, the only technique you need. In harder puzzles every elimination made by an advanced technique usually leaves a naked single behind, so check for them after every step.
spot: Look at cells with many placed peers: a cell in a row that already has seven digits, or a cell whose row, column and box together cover eight different digits. Without notes, count the digits you can see from the cell. With notes, a naked single is simply a cell showing one candidate, which is why Fill notes makes them easy to find.

steps: Look at {cell}. It is empty, so list every digit that is already placed in its row, its column and its box.
Row {row} contains {rowDigits}. Column {col} contains {colDigits}. Box {box} contains {boxDigits}.
Together they rule out every digit except {d}, so {d} is the only candidate left in {cell}.
Write {d} in {cell}. Then check whether the new digit creates another single in the same row, column or box.

mistakes: Counting only the row or only the box. The eight excluded digits usually come from all three units together.
Forgetting that a digit you placed a moment ago also excludes candidates from its 20 peers; new naked singles appear right after each placement.
Confusing a naked single with a hidden single: a naked single has one candidate left in the cell, a hidden single has one cell left for the digit in a unit.
faq: What is a naked single in Sudoku?
An empty cell with exactly one candidate. Eight different digits are already placed in its row, column and box, so the ninth digit is the only one that fits.
Why is it called naked?

Because the single candidate is visible directly in the cell once the notes are written; nothing hides it. A hidden single, by contrast, sits among other candidates and is found by looking at the digit rather than the cell.
Can a puzzle be solved with naked singles only?

Many Easy puzzles can, but most also need hidden singles. Bare Sudoku rates Easy and Medium puzzles as solvable with singles of both kinds; Hard and Expert puzzles need at least one further technique.
Does the hint show naked singles?
Yes. When the next placement is a naked single, the hint selects the cell and says "Only one candidate here" with the digit. Tap the hint again to place it.

hidden-single.name: Hidden single
hidden-single.title: Hidden Single in Sudoku: The Only Place for a Digit
hidden-single.description: A hidden single is the only cell in a row, column or box where a digit can still go. Learn to spot hidden singles by scanning one digit at a time.
hidden-single.summary: A hidden single is a digit that has only one possible cell left in a row, column or box, even though that cell may show other candidates. Because the unit must contain the digit, it goes there. The Bare Sudoku hint reports it as "Only place for 5 in this row", column or box.
when: Whenever a digit is well advanced: once a digit appears five or six times, the remaining boxes are very constrained, and a hidden single is often the next move. Hidden singles are the main technique of Easy and Medium puzzles and remain the workhorse at every level.
spot: Scan one digit at a time. Take a digit, find a box that does not contain it, and cross out every cell of that box that shares a row or column with a placed copy of the digit. If one cell survives, you have found a hidden single. The same scan works on rows and columns. In the game, tap a placed digit: every copy of it is highlighted, so the free cells stand out.

steps: Box {box} does not contain {d} yet, so one of its empty cells must hold it. The empty cells are {empties}.
In every one of them except {cell}, {d} is blocked by a {d} already placed in the same row or column, so {d} is not a candidate there.
That leaves {cell} as the only place for {d} in box {box}. Write {d} there, even though {cell} may still show other candidates.

mistakes: Placing the digit in a cell that is only probably the right one: check every other empty cell of the unit, not just the obvious ones.
Missing a hidden single because the cell shows several candidates. The other candidates do not matter; what matters is that the digit has no other place in the unit.
Scanning only boxes. Rows and columns produce hidden singles just as often, especially near the end.
faq: What is a hidden single in Sudoku?
A digit that can go in only one cell of a row, column or box. The unit must contain the digit, so the cell is decided even if it still has other candidates.
What is the difference between a hidden single and a naked single?
A naked single is about a cell: one candidate left. A hidden single is about a digit: one cell left in a unit. Both place a digit with certainty.
Which is easier to find?

Without notes, hidden singles are usually easier because you can scan the board for one digit at a time. With complete notes, naked singles are the easiest, since a cell with a single candidate stands out.
How does the hint describe a hidden single?
As "Only place for" the digit in this row, this column or this box, with the cell selected. Tap the hint again to place it.

locked-candidates.name: Locked candidates
locked-candidates.title: Locked Candidates in Sudoku: Pointing and Claiming
locked-candidates.description: Locked candidates: when a digit's candidates in a box all lie in one row or column, or the reverse, the digit is removed elsewhere. Two real examples.
locked-candidates.summary: Locked candidates is the first technique that removes candidates instead of placing a digit. It has two forms. Pointing: in a box, all candidates for a digit lie in one row or column, so the digit is removed from the rest of that line. Claiming: in a row or column, all candidates for a digit lie in one box, so the digit is removed from the rest of that box. The Bare Sudoku hint labels the placement it unlocks with "Locked candidates".
when: When singles run out in a Hard puzzle, this is the first thing to try. It needs complete notes for at least the digit you examine. Locked candidates are common: most Hard puzzles need them, and Expert puzzles use them between the bigger patterns.
spot: For pointing, look at each box and each digit missing from it: if the candidate cells for that digit sit in a single row or column, check whether the same digit appears as a candidate further along that line outside the box. For claiming, look along a row or column: if the candidates for a digit are all inside one box, the rest of that box can be cleared. In the game, tap a digit key to highlight every candidate for it; a line of two or three highlighted notes inside one box is the pattern.

steps: In box {box}, digit {d} has only these candidate cells: {cells}. All of them lie in row {row}.
Box {box} needs a {d}, so the {d} of row {row} is inside box {box}, whichever of those cells it lands in.
Row {row} cannot hold a second {d}, so remove {d} from the cells of row {row} outside the box: {elim}.
In row {row}, digit {d} can only go in {cells}, and they all sit inside box {box}.
Row {row} must contain {d}, so the {d} of box {box} is claimed by row {row}. The other cells of box {box} cannot hold {d}.
Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Removing the digit inside the box instead of outside it in the pointing case, or the other way round in the claiming case. The eliminations always go to the cells that are in the line but not in the box, or in the box but not in the line.
Applying the rule when the candidates span two rows of the box. All candidate cells for the digit in the box must lie in one line.
Forgetting to look for the single that the elimination creates. Locked candidates rarely place a digit by themselves; they set up a single.
faq: What are locked candidates in Sudoku?

Candidates for a digit that are confined to the intersection of a box and a line. Since the box, or the line, must contain the digit within that intersection, the digit can be removed from the rest of the line, or the rest of the box.
What is the difference between pointing and claiming?

Pointing starts from a box: the digit's candidates in the box point along one row or column, so the digit is removed from the rest of that line. Claiming starts from a row or column: the line's candidates for the digit are all in one box, so the line claims the digit and it is removed from the rest of the box.
Are locked candidates also called intersection removal?
Yes. Other names are box-line reduction for the claiming form and pointing pairs or pointing triples for the pointing form. Bare Sudoku uses one name for both.
Which level needs locked candidates?
Hard. A puzzle that needs locked candidates or subsets but nothing harder is rated Hard; Expert puzzles also need an advanced pattern, such as a fish or a wing.

naked-pairs.name: Naked pairs and triples
naked-pairs.title: Naked Pairs and Triples in Sudoku: How They Work
naked-pairs.description: Naked pairs and triples: two or three cells in a unit that share the same two or three candidates. Learn to spot them and what to remove, with real examples.
naked-pairs.h1: Naked pairs and triples
naked-pairs.summary: A naked pair is two cells in the same row, column or box that have exactly the same two candidates. The two digits must go in those two cells, so they can be removed from every other cell of the unit. A naked triple is the same idea with three cells and three digits; each cell may show two or all three of them. The Bare Sudoku hint labels the resulting placement "Pair or triple".
when: After the notes are complete and singles and locked candidates are exhausted. Naked pairs are very common in Hard puzzles, naked triples less so. Both are worth checking in every unit that still has five or more empty cells.
spot: Look for cells with only two candidates and find another cell in the same unit with the same two. For triples, look at units with several two- and three-candidate cells and check whether three of them together use only three different digits. Cells with exactly the same candidates are easy to see once the notes are written; Fill notes in the game does that in one tap.

steps: {cellA} and {cellB} in {unit} have exactly the same two candidates: {d1} and {d2}.
One of them must be {d1} and the other {d2}. We do not know which, but both digits are used up by these two cells.
So no other cell of {unit} can hold {d1} or {d2}. Remove {elim}.
Three cells of {unit} draw all their candidates from the same three digits, {digits}: {cells}.
The three digits must fill these three cells in some order. A cell does not need to show all three candidates; what matters is that none of the three cells has a candidate outside the set.
Remove {digits} from every other cell of {unit}: {elim}.

mistakes: Taking two cells that share two candidates but also have a third one. For a naked pair, each cell must have exactly the two candidates and nothing else.
Removing the digits from the pair cells themselves. The pair keeps its candidates; the eliminations go to the other cells of the unit.
Requiring every cell of a triple to show all three digits. A cell with two of the three is fine, as long as no cell has a candidate outside the set.
faq: What is a naked pair in Sudoku?
Two cells in one unit that both have exactly the same two candidates. Those two digits are locked into those two cells, so they can be removed from the rest of the unit.
What is a naked triple?

Three cells in one unit whose candidates together are only three digits. Each cell may hold two or three of them. The three digits fill the three cells, so they can be removed from the other cells of the unit.
Does a naked pair place a digit?
Not by itself. It removes candidates, and the removal usually leaves a naked or hidden single. The hint in Bare Sudoku shows that single and names the technique that made it possible.
Can a naked pair be in a box and a row at the same time?
Yes. If the two cells share a row and a box, the pair eliminates in both units. Bare Sudoku handles them one unit at a time.

hidden-pairs.name: Hidden pairs and triples
hidden-pairs.title: Hidden Pairs and Triples in Sudoku: How to Spot Them
hidden-pairs.description: A hidden pair is two digits that can only go in the same two cells of a unit, so their other candidates go. Learn to find hidden pairs and triples step by step.
hidden-pairs.h1: Hidden pairs and triples
hidden-pairs.summary: A hidden pair is two digits that, within one row, column or box, are candidates in the same two cells and nowhere else. Those two cells must hold those two digits, so every other candidate in them can be removed. A hidden triple works the same way with three digits confined to three cells. After the removal the cells show a naked pair or triple. The Bare Sudoku hint labels the resulting placement "Pair or triple".
when: When a unit has cells with many candidates and singles are gone. Hidden pairs hide inside busy cells, which is why they are worth looking for exactly where naked pairs are not visible. Hidden triples are rare; Bare Sudoku checks for them, but most Hard puzzles are solved without.
spot: Work by digit, not by cell. In a unit, note the cells where each missing digit can go. If two digits each have only two possible cells and they are the same two cells, you have a hidden pair. In the game, tap a digit key to highlight its candidates; if two digits light up the same two cells of a unit and nothing else in it, that is the pattern.

steps: In {unit}, digits {d1} and {d2} each have only two possible cells, and they are the same two: {cells}.
Those two cells must hold {d1} and {d2}, so their other candidates are impossible.
Remove {elim}. Now the two cells show a naked pair, which may unlock more.

mistakes: Removing the two pair digits from the pair cells. It is the other candidates of those cells that go; the pair digits stay.
Accepting a digit that has a third possible cell in the unit. Both digits must be limited to exactly the two cells.
Looking only in boxes. Hidden pairs occur just as often in rows and columns.
faq: What is a hidden pair in Sudoku?
Two digits that can go in only the same two cells of a unit. Those cells must take those digits, so their other candidates are removed.
How is a hidden pair different from a naked pair?
A naked pair is visible: two cells that show only the same two candidates. A hidden pair is covered by extra candidates in the two cells. Removing those extras turns a hidden pair into a naked pair.
What is a hidden triple?
Three digits confined to three cells of a unit. Each digit need not appear in all three cells; what matters is that none of the three digits has a candidate outside those cells.
Does the hint distinguish hidden and naked pairs?
No. Bare Sudoku finds both and labels the resulting placement "Pair or triple". The pages here separate them because they are found in different ways.

x-wing.name: X-Wing
x-wing.title: X-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
x-wing.description: X-Wing: a digit with exactly two candidate cells in two rows, lined up in the same two columns, is removed from the rest of those columns. Real example.
x-wing.summary: An X-Wing is a pattern of one digit and four cells at the corners of a rectangle. If the digit has exactly two candidate cells in each of two rows, and those cells lie in the same two columns, then the digit must occupy two opposite corners of the rectangle. It can therefore be removed from every other cell of those two columns. The same works with rows and columns swapped. It is the first Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When singles, locked candidates and subsets are exhausted. The X-Wing is the first Expert pattern to look for and often appears when a digit has few candidates left, typically with four to six copies already placed. It needs complete notes for the digit you examine.
spot: Choose a digit and look for rows in which it has exactly two candidate cells. If two such rows share the same two columns, check those columns for other candidates of the digit: those are the eliminations. Then repeat with columns as the base. In the game, tap the digit key: every candidate for it is highlighted, and a rectangle of four highlighted notes is easy to see.

steps: Digit {d} has exactly two candidate cells in row {r1} and exactly two in row {r2}, and they line up in the same two columns, {c1} and {c2}: {cells}.
Row {r1} puts its {d} in column {c1} or {c2}, and row {r2} puts its {d} in the other one. Either way, columns {c1} and {c2} each receive a {d} from these two rows.
So {d} cannot appear anywhere else in columns {c1} and {c2}. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using a row that has three candidate cells for the digit. Each base row must have exactly two, and both must be in the two shared columns.
Removing the digit from the rows instead of the columns. With rows as the base, the eliminations are in the columns, and vice versa.
Forgetting the swapped version. An X-Wing built on columns eliminates in rows.
faq: What is an X-Wing in Sudoku?

A digit that has exactly two candidate cells in each of two rows, in the same two columns. The digit occupies two opposite corners of that rectangle, so it is removed from the rest of the two columns. Rows and columns can be swapped.
Why does an X-Wing work?

Each of the two rows must place the digit in one of the two columns, and the two rows cannot use the same column. So the two columns each receive their copy of the digit from these rows, and every other candidate in those columns is impossible.
Is an X-Wing a fish?
Yes. The X-Wing is the fish of size two; Swordfish is the fish of size three. Bare Sudoku finds both.
Which level has X-Wings?

Expert or Master. Bare Sudoku rates a puzzle as Expert when it needs an X-Wing or another advanced pattern, such as the Y-Wing or the Skyscraper, and as Master when it also needs chains or other techniques beyond this guide.

swordfish.name: Swordfish
swordfish.title: Swordfish in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
swordfish.description: Swordfish: a digit confined to three columns across three rows is removed from the rest of those columns. The size-three fish, explained with a real example.
swordfish.summary: A Swordfish is an X-Wing with three rows and three columns. If a digit has at most three candidate cells in each of three rows, and all of those cells fall in the same three columns, then the three rows use up the digit in those columns, and the digit can be removed from every other cell of the three columns. Rows and columns can be swapped. Bare Sudoku checks for Swordfish right after X-Wing, in Expert puzzles.
when: When an X-Wing finds nothing. Swordfish are less common than X-Wings and need a digit whose candidates are spread thinly over three lines. They need complete and accurate notes for that digit.
spot: Pick a digit and look for rows with two or three candidate cells for it. If three such rows cover only three columns in total, check those columns for further candidates of the digit. Not every row needs a candidate in every column: a Swordfish can have six, seven, eight or nine cells. In the game, highlight the digit with its key and look for three rows whose candidates line up in three columns.

steps: Digit {d} has at most three candidate cells in each of rows {rows}, and all of those cells fall in columns {cols}: {cells}.
Each of the three rows must place its {d} in one of the three columns, and no two rows can use the same column. So the three columns get their {d} from these three rows.
Any other {d} candidate in columns {cols} is impossible. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Requiring all nine cells. A Swordfish with two candidates in some rows is still valid, as long as the three rows cover only three columns.
Including a row with four candidate cells. Each base row must have at most three, all within the three columns.
Eliminating in the base rows. With rows as the base, the eliminations are in the three columns, outside the base rows.
faq: What is a Swordfish in Sudoku?

A digit whose candidates in three rows are confined to three columns. The three rows must place the digit in those three columns, one each, so the digit is removed from the other cells of those columns.
How is a Swordfish different from an X-Wing?
Only in size: an X-Wing uses two rows and two columns, a Swordfish three and three. The reasoning is the same.
Does a Swordfish need exactly nine cells?
No. Each row can have two or three candidates; the pattern only requires that the three rows together use no more than three columns.
Is there a fish of size four?
Yes, the Jellyfish, with four rows and four columns. The reasoning is the same as for the X-Wing and the Swordfish, only with more lines.

skyscraper.name: Skyscraper
skyscraper.title: Skyscraper in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
skyscraper.description: Skyscraper: a digit with exactly two candidates in each of two rows, aligned in one column only, is removed from cells seeing both other ends. Real example.
skyscraper.summary: A Skyscraper is a single-digit pattern built on two rows in which a digit has exactly two candidate cells. One cell of each row lies in the same column; these two cells are the base, and they cannot both hold the digit. The other two cells, the tops, lie in different columns. Because at least one base cell is not the digit, at least one top must be, so the digit can be removed from every cell that sees both tops. The same works with columns instead of rows. The Skyscraper is a form of Turbot Fish, like the [2-String Kite](two-string-kite), and it is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When X-Wing and Swordfish find nothing. The Skyscraper is one of the most common Expert patterns in Bare Sudoku, and it often appears where an [X-Wing](x-wing) almost works: two rows with two candidates each for a digit, sharing only one column instead of two. It needs complete notes for the digit you examine.
spot: Pick a digit and list the rows in which it has exactly two candidate cells. Compare those rows in pairs: if exactly one candidate cell of each row sits in the same column, those two cells are the base and the other two are the tops. Then look for cells that see both tops and still contain the digit; usually they sit in the box of one top and the column of the other. Repeat with columns instead of rows. In the game, tap the digit key to highlight its candidates and look for two rows that show exactly two each.

steps: Digit {d} has exactly two candidate cells in row {r1}, {baseA} and {topA}, and exactly two in row {r2}, {baseB} and {topB}.
{baseA} and {baseB} are both in column {col}, so at most one of them can be {d}. They form the base; {topA} and {topB} are the tops.
If {baseA} is not {d}, row {r1} must put its {d} in {topA}. If {baseB} is not {d}, row {r2} must put its {d} in {topB}. At least one base cell is not {d}, so at least one top is {d}.
A cell that sees both tops can never be {d}. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using a row that has three candidate cells for the digit. Each of the two rows must have exactly two, or the row could place the digit somewhere else.
Taking two rows whose candidates line up in both columns. That is an X-Wing, which removes the digit from the rest of the two columns instead.
Removing the digit from cells that see only one top. The eliminated cell must see both tops.
faq: What is a Skyscraper in Sudoku?

A pattern of one digit in two rows, or two columns, where the digit has exactly two candidate cells each. One cell of each row lines up in a shared column; the other two, the tops, do not. At least one top holds the digit, so it is removed from every cell that sees both tops.
Why is it called a Skyscraper?
Because of its shape in the column version: two columns rise from a shared base row like two towers, and their tops end at different heights. The row version is the same pattern turned on its side.
Is a Skyscraper a Turbot Fish?

Yes. A Turbot Fish joins two units in which a digit has exactly two candidates through two cells that see each other. In a Skyscraper the two units are parallel rows or parallel columns, and the joined cells share a column or a row; in a 2-String Kite they are a row and a column joined in a box.
How is a Skyscraper different from an X-Wing?

An X-Wing needs both pairs of candidates to line up in the same two columns, and it removes the digit from the rest of those columns. A Skyscraper lines up only one pair; the tops are free, and only cells that see both tops lose the digit.

two-string-kite.name: 2-String Kite
two-string-kite.title: 2-String Kite in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
two-string-kite.description: 2-String Kite: a digit with two candidates in a row and two in a column, joined in one box, is removed from cells that see both free ends. Real example.
two-string-kite.summary: A 2-String Kite is a single-digit pattern made of one row and one column in which a digit has exactly two candidate cells each. One cell of the row and one cell of the column lie in the same box, so at most one of them holds the digit. Therefore at least one of the two other cells, the ends of the kite, holds it, and the digit can be removed from every cell that sees both ends. Like the [Skyscraper](skyscraper), it is a form of Turbot Fish, and it is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When the [Skyscraper](skyscraper) and the patterns before it find nothing. 2-String Kites are less common than Skyscrapers. Look for them when a digit is down to two candidates in a row and two in a column, with one candidate of each in the same box. They need complete notes for that digit.
spot: Pick a digit and find a row where it has exactly two candidate cells and a column where it has exactly two, with no cell in common. If one cell of the row and one cell of the column share a box, the two remaining cells are the ends of the kite. Then look at the cells that see both ends; usually there is just one, in the row of one end and the column of the other. In the game, tap the digit key: the row and the column each show two highlighted notes.

steps: Digit {d} has exactly two candidate cells in row {row}, {rowInBox} and {rowEnd}, and exactly two in column {col}, {colInBox} and {colEnd}.
{rowInBox} and {colInBox} are both in box {box}, so at most one of them can be {d}.

If {rowInBox} is not {d}, row {row} must put its {d} in {rowEnd}. If {colInBox} is not {d}, column {col} must put its {d} in {colEnd}. At least one of the two box cells is not {d}, so {rowEnd} or {colEnd} is {d}.
A cell that sees both {rowEnd} and {colEnd} can never be {d}. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using a row or a column with three candidate cells for the digit. Both strings must have exactly two.
Joining the strings through cells in different boxes. The pattern only works because the two inner cells share a box, so they cannot both hold the digit.
Removing the digit from the box that joins the strings, or from cells that see only one end. Only cells that see both ends lose the digit.
faq: What is a 2-String Kite in Sudoku?

A pattern of one digit with exactly two candidate cells in a row and exactly two in a column. One cell of the row and one of the column share a box, so at least one of the other two cells holds the digit, and it is removed from every cell that sees both of them.
Why is it called a 2-String Kite?
The row and the column are the two strings, each holding exactly two candidates, and the box where they meet ties them together. Drawn on the grid, the two strings and the box look like a kite.
Is a 2-String Kite a Turbot Fish?

Yes. Like the Skyscraper, it joins two units in which the digit has exactly two candidates through two cells that see each other. In the kite the units are a row and a column, and the two joined cells share a box.
How is a 2-String Kite different from a Skyscraper?

A Skyscraper uses two parallel lines, two rows or two columns, joined in a shared column or row. A 2-String Kite uses one row and one column joined in a box. The reasoning and the eliminations work the same way.

y-wing.name: Y-Wing
y-wing.title: Y-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
y-wing.description: Y-Wing (XY-Wing): a pivot with two candidates and two wings that each share one of them force a digit out of every cell that sees both wings. Example.
y-wing.summary: A Y-Wing, also called XY-Wing, uses three cells with two candidates each. The pivot has candidates X and Y. One wing sees the pivot and has X and Z; the other wing sees the pivot and has Y and Z. Whatever the pivot is, one of the wings must be Z, so Z can be removed from every cell that sees both wings. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When a puzzle has several cells with exactly two candidates and no fish is available. Y-Wings are common in Expert puzzles and are found by following the two-candidate cells: each is a potential pivot or wing.
spot: List the cells with exactly two candidates. For each one, treat it as the pivot with candidates X and Y, and look among its peers for a cell with X and another digit Z, and a cell with Y and the same Z. Those two are the wings. Then find cells that see both wings and contain Z. Note that the wings do not need to see each other.

steps: The pivot {pivot} has candidates {x} and {y}. It sees {wingA}, which has {x} and {z}, and {wingB}, which has {y} and {z}.
If {pivot} is {x}, then {wingA} loses {x} and becomes {z}. If {pivot} is {y}, then {wingB} becomes {z}. One of the two wings is {z} in every case.
A cell that sees both wings can never be {z}. Remove {z} from {elim}.

mistakes: Choosing wings that do not both see the pivot. Each wing must share a row, column or box with the pivot.
Removing Z from cells that see only one wing. The eliminated cell must see both wings.
Removing Z from the pivot. The pivot does not contain Z in a Y-Wing; if it does, the pattern is an XYZ-Wing with different rules.
faq: What is a Y-Wing in Sudoku?

Three two-candidate cells: a pivot with X and Y, a wing with X and Z that sees the pivot, and a wing with Y and Z that sees the pivot. One wing is always Z, so Z is removed from cells that see both wings.
Is Y-Wing the same as XY-Wing?
Yes. The two names describe the same pattern. Bare Sudoku calls it Y-Wing.
Why must one wing be Z?
If the pivot is X, the first wing loses X and becomes Z. If the pivot is Y, the second wing becomes Z. The pivot is one of the two, so one wing is Z.
How many cells does a Y-Wing eliminate?
Usually one or two: only the cells that see both wings and still contain Z. That is enough to create a single.

xyz-wing.name: XYZ-Wing
xyz-wing.title: XYZ-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
xyz-wing.description: XYZ-Wing: a pivot with three candidates and two wings that share one of them force that digit out of every cell seeing all three. Real example, step by step.
xyz-wing.summary: An XYZ-Wing is a Y-Wing whose pivot has three candidates. The pivot has X, Y and Z; one wing sees the pivot and has X and Z, the other sees the pivot and has Y and Z. One of the three cells must be Z, so Z can be removed from every cell that sees all three. Because the pivot itself may be Z, the eliminated cell must see the pivot as well as both wings, which limits it to the box or line the cells share. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When X-Wing, Y-Wing and Swordfish find nothing. XYZ-Wings are less common than Y-Wings. Look for them when a three-candidate cell sits in a box with a two-candidate cell that shares two of its digits.
spot: Start from cells with exactly three candidates; each is a possible pivot. Among its peers, look for two cells with two candidates each, both taken from the pivot's three, sharing exactly one digit Z. Then look for cells that see the pivot and both wings and contain Z. In practice one wing is in the pivot's box and the other in its row or column, and the eliminated cells are the remaining cells of that box in that row or column.

steps: The pivot {pivot} has three candidates: {x}, {y} and {z}. It sees {wingA} with {x} and {z}, and {wingB} with {y} and {z}.
If {pivot} is {z}, done. If it is {x}, {wingA} must be {z}. If it is {y}, {wingB} must be {z}. In every case one of the three cells is {z}.
A cell that sees all three cannot be {z}. Remove {z} from {elim}.

mistakes: Eliminating from cells that see only the two wings. Unlike a Y-Wing, the pivot can be Z, so the cell must see the pivot too.
Using wings whose candidates are not both contained in the pivot's three candidates.
Confusing it with a Y-Wing: the difference is the third candidate in the pivot, and it changes which cells can be cleared.
faq: What is an XYZ-Wing in Sudoku?
A pivot with candidates X, Y and Z and two wings, one with X and Z and one with Y and Z, both seeing the pivot. One of the three cells is Z, so Z is removed from cells that see all three.
How is an XYZ-Wing different from a Y-Wing?
The pivot has three candidates instead of two, including Z. That makes the pivot a possible home for Z, so only cells that see the pivot and both wings can lose Z.
How often does an XYZ-Wing appear?
Less often than a Y-Wing: most Expert puzzles in Bare Sudoku are solved without one. The solver looks for it after X-Wing, Y-Wing and Swordfish.
Is there a WXYZ-Wing?
Yes: four cells with four candidates in two crossing units, where one digit is free to sit in more than one of them. Bare Sudoku finds it too and rates it Expert, like the other wings.

w-wing.name: W-Wing
w-wing.title: W-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
w-wing.description: W-Wing: two cells with the same two candidates, linked by a digit that has only two places in a unit, remove the other digit from cells that see both.
w-wing.summary: A W-Wing uses two cells that have exactly the same two candidates, X and Z, and do not see each other. They are joined by a strong link on X: a row, column or box in which X has exactly two candidate cells, one seeing each of the two pair cells. If both pair cells were X, that unit would have no place left for X, so at least one of them is Z. Z can therefore be removed from every cell that sees both pair cells. The W-Wing is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When single-digit patterns such as the [Skyscraper](skyscraper) and the [2-String Kite](two-string-kite) find nothing. W-Wings are less common than [Y-Wings](y-wing) but appear regularly in Expert puzzles. Look for them when two cells far apart show the same pair of candidates.
spot: List the cells with exactly two candidates and look for two with the same pair, say X and Z, that share no row, column or box. For each of the two digits, look for a row, column or box where it has exactly two candidate cells, one seeing each pair cell. If X has such a link, check the cells that see both pair cells: they lose Z. Then try the same with a link on Z, which would remove X.

steps: {wingA} and {wingB} both have exactly the candidates {x} and {z}, and they do not see each other.
In {unit}, digit {x} has only two candidate cells: {linkA}, which sees {wingA}, and {linkB}, which sees {wingB}. One of them must be {x}.
If {wingA} and {wingB} were both {x}, neither {linkA} nor {linkB} could be {x}, and {unit} would have no place for {x}. So at least one of {wingA} and {wingB} is {z}.
A cell that sees both {wingA} and {wingB} can never be {z}. Remove {z} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using a link unit in which X has three or more candidate cells. X must have exactly two places in that unit, one seeing each pair cell.
Removing X instead of Z. The link is on X, so the digit that is removed is the other candidate, Z.
Using two pair cells that see each other. They are then a naked pair, a simpler technique that removes both digits from the unit they share.
faq: What is a W-Wing in Sudoku?

Two cells with the same two candidates, X and Z, that do not see each other, plus a row, column or box where X has exactly two candidate cells, one seeing each of them. At least one of the two cells is Z, so Z is removed from every cell that sees both.
Why does a W-Wing work?
If both pair cells were X, they would rule X out of both link cells, and the link unit would have nowhere to put X. So at least one pair cell is Z, and a cell that sees both of them cannot be Z.
How is a W-Wing different from a Y-Wing?

A Y-Wing connects its two wings through a pivot cell with two candidates. A W-Wing connects two cells with identical candidates through a strong link, a unit where one of their digits has only two places. Both remove a digit from the cells that see both ends.
Can the link of a W-Wing be in a box?
Yes. The link can be any row, column or box in which X has exactly two candidate cells, as long as one of them sees each pair cell.

unique-rectangle.name: Unique Rectangle
unique-rectangle.title: Unique Rectangle in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
unique-rectangle.description: Unique Rectangle: when three corners of a rectangle in two boxes hold only the same two candidates, the fourth loses them, or there would be two solutions.
unique-rectangle.summary: A Unique Rectangle is a uniqueness technique: it relies on the fact that a proper Sudoku has exactly one solution. Four empty cells at the corners of a rectangle, in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes, can never be filled with just two digits A and B, because A and B could then be swapped in all four corners and the puzzle would have two solutions. So when three corners have exactly the candidates A and B and the fourth has A, B and more, the fourth corner cannot be A or B, and both are removed from it. This page explains Type 1, the form the Bare Sudoku solver uses. The argument is valid because every Bare Sudoku puzzle is checked to have exactly one solution.
when: When three corners of a rectangle are down to the same two candidates and the simpler patterns find nothing. Unique Rectangles are rare: only a small share of Bare Sudoku puzzles need one. They need complete notes, at least for the four corners.
spot: Look for two cells in the same row with exactly the same two candidates, then for a third cell with that pair in the column of one of them. The fourth corner completes the rectangle. Check that the four cells lie in exactly two boxes and that the fourth corner has the pair plus at least one other candidate; then remove the pair from it. A rectangle spread over four boxes proves nothing, because swapping its digits would break the boxes.

steps: The empty cells {corners} are the corners of a rectangle in two rows and two columns, and they lie in exactly two boxes, {boxA} and {boxB}.
Three corners, {pairCells}, have exactly the candidates {a} and {b}. The fourth corner, {target}, has {a} and {b} plus {extra}.

If {target} were {a} or {b}, all four corners would hold only {a} and {b}, and swapping the two digits in them would give a second solution. Every Bare Sudoku puzzle has exactly one solution, so this cannot happen.
So {target} is neither {a} nor {b}. Remove {a} and {b} from {target}; it keeps {extra}.

mistakes: Using a rectangle whose corners lie in four boxes. Swapping the digits would then break the boxes, so there is no second solution to avoid and nothing to remove.
Removing the pair from the three corners that hold only it. The eliminations happen only in the fourth corner, the one with extra candidates.

Using the technique on a puzzle that may have more than one solution. It relies on uniqueness; Bare Sudoku checks every puzzle for exactly one solution, but a puzzle from elsewhere may not be checked.
faq: What is a Unique Rectangle in Sudoku?

A pattern of four empty cells at the corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes. If three corners hold only the candidates A and B, the fourth corner cannot be A or B, because otherwise the puzzle would have two solutions, so A and B are removed from it.
Why is it safe to rely on uniqueness?

Because a proper Sudoku has exactly one solution, and Bare Sudoku checks that every puzzle it generates has exactly one. If the four corners held only A and B, swapping them would give a second solution, which cannot exist, so the fourth corner must take another digit.
Which type of Unique Rectangle does Bare Sudoku use?

Type 1, described on this page: three corners with exactly the same two candidates and a fourth corner with those two plus others. Bare Sudoku also finds the other types, usually numbered 2 to 6, which use extra candidates in two or more corners or strong links between them, and the Hidden Rectangle.
What is a deadly pattern?

Four corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes that hold the same two digits crosswise. The digits could be swapped without breaking any rule, so a puzzle with one solution never ends up with one. Unique Rectangles remove the candidates that would create it.

finned-x-wing.name: Finned X-Wing
finned-x-wing.title: Finned X-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
finned-x-wing.description: Finned X-Wing: an X-Wing with an extra candidate, the fin, in a base row. The digit is removed from the cover cells that lie in the fin's box. Real example.
finned-x-wing.summary: A Finned X-Wing is an [X-Wing](x-wing) that almost works: a digit has candidates in two rows that line up in two columns, except for one or more extra cells, the fins, in one of the two rows. All fins must lie in the same box. Either a fin holds the digit, or no fin does and the plain X-Wing applies; in both cases the digit cannot sit in the cells of the two cover columns that lie in the fin's box, outside the base rows, so it is removed from them. Rows and columns can be swapped. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When an X-Wing almost appears: two rows with the digit lined up in two columns plus a stray candidate or two in a single box. Finned X-Wings are among the most common Expert patterns in Bare Sudoku, and they need complete notes for the digit you examine.
spot: Pick a digit and look for rows in which it has two or three candidate cells. Take two such rows and find two columns that cover all of their candidates except one or two cells; those cells are the fins, and they must sit in one box. Then look at the cells of the two columns inside the fin's box, outside the two rows: any that contain the digit lose it. Repeat with columns as the base. In the game, tap the digit key: a near rectangle of highlighted notes with an extra note beside it is the sign.

steps: Digit {d} has candidates in rows {r1} and {r2} only in columns {c1} and {c2}, apart from one extra cell, {fin}, in box {finBox}. Without {fin} the pattern would be an X-Wing.
If {fin} is not {d}, the X-Wing holds: rows {r1} and {r2} place their {d} in columns {c1} and {c2}, and no other cell of those columns can be {d}.
If {fin} is {d}, no other cell of box {finBox} can be {d}.
A cell of column {c1} or {c2} that lies in box {finBox}, outside rows {r1} and {r2}, is ruled out either way. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Removing the digit from the whole of the two columns, as in a plain X-Wing. With a fin, only the cover cells inside the fin's box can be cleared.
Using fins in two different boxes. The eliminated cells must see every fin, and cells in one box cannot see fins in two.
Taking a candidate outside the base rows for a fin. Fins lie in the base rows; an extra candidate in a cover column outside them is a cell the X-Wing would eliminate.
faq: What is a Finned X-Wing in Sudoku?

An X-Wing with extra candidates, called fins, in one of its two base rows, all inside one box. Either a fin is the digit, or the X-Wing is valid; both cases rule out the digit in the cells of the cover columns that lie in the fin's box, so it is removed from them.
What is a fin?

A candidate cell in a base row of a fish that lies outside the cover columns. A fish with fins eliminates only in cells that see every fin, which is why all fins of a Finned X-Wing must lie in one box.
What is a Sashimi X-Wing?

A Finned X-Wing in which a base row keeps only one candidate in the cover columns once the fins are set aside. The reasoning is the same: either a fin holds the digit, or the rows force it into the cover columns. Bare Sudoku reports both as a Finned X-Wing.
How is a Finned X-Wing different from a Skyscraper?

Both use a digit in two rows. A Skyscraper needs exactly two candidates per row, aligned in one column, and eliminates in the cells that see both free ends. A Finned X-Wing needs the candidates aligned in two columns with the extra cells confined to one box, and eliminates only inside that box. Every Skyscraper can also be read as a fish with a fin; Bare Sudoku tries the Skyscraper first because it is easier to see.

empty-rectangle.name: Empty Rectangle
empty-rectangle.title: Empty Rectangle in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
empty-rectangle.description: Empty Rectangle: a box where a digit's candidates lie in one row and one column, joined to a strong link, rules the digit out of one cell at the far end.
empty-rectangle.summary: An Empty Rectangle is a single-digit pattern. In one box, every candidate for a digit lies in a single row or a single column of that box; the four cells outside those two lines hold no candidate, which gives the pattern its name. The box is joined to a strong link: a row or column outside the box's band or stack in which the digit has exactly two candidate cells, one of them in the box's row or column. Then the cell that sees the other end of that link and lies on the box's other line can never be the digit, and it is removed from that cell. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When a digit's candidates in a box form an L or a T along one row and one column, and the digit also has a row or column with exactly two candidates nearby. Empty Rectangles are common in Expert puzzles, about as common as Finned X-Wings. They need complete notes for the digit.
spot: Pick a digit and look at each box where it has at least two candidate cells. If all of them fit in one row plus one column of the box, you have an empty rectangle for that digit. Now find a column outside the box's stack where the digit has exactly two candidate cells, one of them in the box's row; the other end of that column is the far cell. The cell in the far cell's row and the box's column loses the digit. Try the same with a row outside the box's band and the box's column. In the game, tap the digit key and look for a box whose highlighted notes form an L or a T.

steps: In box {box}, every candidate for {d} lies in row {row} or column {col}. The other four cells of the box hold no {d}: they form the empty rectangle.
In {linkUnit}, {d} has exactly two candidate cells, {linkA} and {linkB}, and {linkA} lies in {erA}. One of the two must be {d}.
If {linkB} is {d}, then {elim} is not {d}, because it sees {linkB}.
If {linkA} is {d}, then {erA} has its {d} outside box {box}, so the box must place {d} in {erB}. {elim} lies in {erB} too, outside the box, so it is not {d} either.
Both cases rule out the same cell. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using a box where the digit has a candidate outside the chosen row and column. Every candidate in the box must lie on one of the two lines.

Taking a link row or column with three candidate cells for the digit, or one that runs through the box's own band or stack. The link must be a strong link outside the box's band or stack, with one end in line with the box.
Removing the digit from the wrong end. The eliminated cell lies on the box's other line, in line with the far end of the link, not next to the box.
faq: What is an Empty Rectangle in Sudoku?

A box in which all candidates for a digit lie in one row and one column, joined to a row or column elsewhere where the digit has exactly two candidate cells, one of them in line with the box. The cell that lies on the box's other line and sees the far end of the pair cannot be the digit.
Why is it called an Empty Rectangle?
Because the four cells of the box that lie outside the chosen row and column contain no candidate for the digit; they form a rectangle that is empty of it.
Why does an Empty Rectangle work?

The two-candidate line forces the digit into one of its two cells. If it is the far cell, the eliminated cell sees it. If it is the near cell, the box must put the digit on its other line, and the eliminated cell lies on that line too. Both cases rule out the same cell.
Is an Empty Rectangle a kind of fish?

It is a close relative: an Empty Rectangle is a grouped Turbot Fish, in which one strong link runs through the box's row and column instead of two single cells. The Skyscraper and the 2-String Kite are its single-cell cousins.

unique-rectangle-type-4.name: Unique Rectangle Type 4
unique-rectangle-type-4.title: Unique Rectangle Type 4 in Sudoku: How It Works
unique-rectangle-type-4.description: Unique Rectangle Type 4: two corners hold only the pair A and B, and A is confined to the other two corners in a shared unit, so B leaves both of them.
unique-rectangle-type-4.summary: A Unique Rectangle Type 4 is a uniqueness technique, like the [Unique Rectangle](unique-rectangle) of Type 1. Four cells at the corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes all hold the candidates A and B; two neighbouring corners, the floor, hold nothing else, and the two opposite them, the roof, hold more. If A has no other candidate cell in a row, column or box that the two roof corners share, one of them must be A. The other cannot then be B, or all four corners would hold only A and B, a deadly pattern with two solutions. So B is removed from both roof corners. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When two neighbouring corners of a rectangle are down to the same pair and the opposite two corners still hold more candidates, so that Type 1 does not apply. Type 4 is the most common of the further Unique Rectangle types in Bare Sudoku puzzles. It needs complete notes for the four corners and for one digit of the pair in the roof's unit.
spot: Find two cells in the same row or column with exactly the same two candidates, A and B, and complete the rectangle with two cells that also hold A and B, in exactly two boxes in total. If the two roof cells still have other candidates, look at the row, column or box they share: if A has no candidate there outside the two roof cells, remove B from both. Then try the same with B as the confined digit, which would remove A.

steps: {corners} are the corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes, {boxA} and {boxB}. All four hold the candidates {a} and {b}.
{floor} hold nothing but {a} and {b}. The other two corners, {roof}, hold {a} and {b} together with other candidates.
In {unit}, {a} has no candidate cell other than {roof}. So one of these two corners must be {a}.

If the other one were {b}, the four corners would hold only {a} and {b}, and swapping the two digits would give a second solution. Every Bare Sudoku puzzle has exactly one solution, so neither corner can be {b}.
Remove {b} from {elim}.

mistakes: Removing A instead of B. The digit that is confined to the two roof cells stays; the other digit of the pair is removed from them.

Using a rectangle whose corners lie in four boxes, or a unit where A has a third candidate cell. Without the two-box shape there is no deadly pattern, and without the strong link on A one roof corner could still be B.
Applying it to a puzzle that may have more than one solution. Every Bare Sudoku puzzle is checked for exactly one solution, so the argument holds in the game.
faq: What is a Unique Rectangle Type 4?

A rectangle of four cells in two rows, two columns and two boxes that all hold the candidates A and B. Two neighbouring corners hold only A and B; the other two hold more, and in a unit they share, A is confined to those two corners. Then B is removed from both of them.
Why does Type 4 work?

One of the two roof corners must be A, because A has nowhere else to go in their shared unit. If the other roof corner were B, all four corners would hold only A and B, and the two digits could be swapped for a second solution. A proper Sudoku has one solution, so B is impossible in both roof corners.
How is Type 4 different from Type 1?

Type 1 has three corners with only the pair and removes both digits from the fourth. Type 4 has two corners with only the pair and uses a strong link on one digit between the other two corners; it removes the other digit from those two.
Which Unique Rectangle types does Bare Sudoku find?
Types 1 to 6 and the Hidden Rectangle. Type 1 and Type 4 are the most common in its puzzles; the hint names the type it used.

hidden-rectangle.name: Hidden Rectangle
hidden-rectangle.title: Hidden Rectangle in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
hidden-rectangle.description: Hidden Rectangle: four corners hold the pair A and B, one of them nothing else, and A is confined to the rectangle in two lines, so the far corner loses B.
hidden-rectangle.summary: A Hidden Rectangle is a uniqueness technique in which the deadly pattern is hidden among other candidates. Four cells at the corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes all hold the candidates A and B, and one corner holds nothing else. In the row and in the column of the opposite corner, A has no candidate cell beyond the corners of the rectangle. If that opposite corner were B, both corners next to it would have to be A, and the first corner would have to be B: the four corners would hold only A and B, a deadly pattern with two solutions. So B is removed from the opposite corner. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When a rectangle's corners all hold the same two candidates, one of them holds nothing else, and the other three still have extra candidates, so that Type 1 and Type 4 do not apply. Hidden Rectangles are about as common as Type 4 in Bare Sudoku puzzles. They need complete notes for one digit of the pair in two lines.
spot: Start from a cell with exactly two candidates, A and B. Look for a rectangle through it, in exactly two boxes, whose other three corners also hold A and B. Take the corner opposite your starting cell and check its row and its column: if A has no candidate there outside the rectangle, that corner loses B. Then try the same with the roles of A and B swapped.

steps: {corners} are the corners of a rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes, {boxA} and {boxB}. All four hold {a} and {b}. {pivot} holds nothing else; the opposite corner, {target}, also holds {extra}.
In row {rowT}, the only candidate cells for {a} are {target} and {sideA}. In column {colT}, they are {target} and {sideB}.

Suppose {target} were {b}. Then {sideA} and {sideB} would both have to be {a}, and {pivot}, which sees both of them, would have to be {b}. The four corners would hold only {a} and {b}, and swapping them would give a second solution.
Every Bare Sudoku puzzle has exactly one solution, so {target} is not {b}. Remove {b} from {target}.

mistakes: Checking the strong links in the wrong cells. The two links on A run through the corner opposite the two-candidate cell, along its row and its column.
Removing A instead of B. The digit with the strong links stays possible; the other digit of the pair is removed from the opposite corner.
Using a rectangle spread over four boxes. Without the two-box shape, swapping the digits would break the boxes and there is no deadly pattern to avoid.
faq: What is a Hidden Rectangle in Sudoku?

A rectangle in two rows, two columns and two boxes whose four corners all hold the candidates A and B, one of them nothing else. If A is confined to the rectangle in both the row and the column of the opposite corner, that corner cannot be B, because the four corners would otherwise hold only A and B and the puzzle would have two solutions.
Why is it called hidden?

Because the deadly pattern is covered by extra candidates in three of the corners. In the plain Unique Rectangle you see three corners with just the pair; here you must look at where the digit A can go in two lines to uncover the pattern.
How is a Hidden Rectangle different from Type 4?

Type 4 needs two neighbouring corners with only the pair and one strong link in the unit of the other two. A Hidden Rectangle needs just one corner with only the pair and two strong links, in the row and the column of the opposite corner.
Can the two-candidate corner be the one that loses B?

No. The strong links run through the row and the column of the corner with extra candidates, and that corner is where B is removed. The corner with only the pair is the one that would be forced to B in the deadly pattern.

finned-swordfish.name: Finned Swordfish
finned-swordfish.title: Finned Swordfish in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
finned-swordfish.description: Finned Swordfish: a Swordfish with an extra candidate, the fin, in a base row. The digit is removed from cover cells that lie in the fin's box. Real example.
finned-swordfish.summary: A Finned Swordfish is a [Swordfish](swordfish) with extra candidates: a digit has candidates in three rows that fall into three columns, except for one or more cells, the fins, which lie together in one box. Either a fin holds the digit, or no fin does and the plain Swordfish applies. In both cases the digit cannot sit in the cells of the three cover columns that lie in the fin's box, outside the base rows, so it is removed from them. Rows and columns can be swapped. It is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When a Swordfish almost appears: three rows whose candidates for a digit fall into three columns apart from a cell or two in one box. Finned Swordfish are less common than Finned X-Wings; look for them when a digit is spread thinly over several rows. They need complete and accurate notes for that digit.
spot: Pick a digit and list the rows with two to four candidate cells for it. Look for three rows and three columns that cover all of their candidates but one or two; the leftover cells are the fins, and they must lie in one box. Then check the cells of the three columns inside the fin's box, outside the three rows: any that hold the digit lose it. Repeat with columns as the base.

steps: Digit {d} has candidates in rows {rows} only in columns {cols}, apart from one extra cell, {fin}, in box {finBox}. Without {fin} the pattern would be a Swordfish.
If {fin} is not {d}, the Swordfish holds: the three rows place their {d} in the three columns, one each, and no other cell of those columns can be {d}.
If {fin} is {d}, no other cell of box {finBox} can be {d}.
A cell of columns {cols} that lies in box {finBox}, outside rows {rows}, is ruled out either way. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Eliminating in the whole of the three columns. With fins, only the cover cells inside the fin's box can be cleared.
Using fins spread over two boxes. All fins must see the eliminated cells, so they must share one box.
Counting a cell outside the base rows as a fin. Fins lie in the base rows; extra candidates elsewhere in the cover columns are cells to eliminate, not fins.
faq: What is a Finned Swordfish in Sudoku?

A Swordfish whose base rows hold extra candidates, the fins, all inside one box. Either a fin is the digit, or the Swordfish is valid; both cases rule out the digit in the cells of the cover columns that lie in the fin's box, so it is removed from them.
How many fins can a Finned Swordfish have?
Bare Sudoku accepts any number, provided they all lie in one box; one or two fins are the norm. Fins in different boxes would leave no cell that sees them all.
Is there a Finned Jellyfish?

Yes: the same idea with four rows and four columns. Bare Sudoku finds Finned Jellyfish as well, but they are rare, because a digit seldom spreads over four rows without a smaller pattern appearing first.
How is a Finned Swordfish different from a Finned X-Wing?
Only in size: a Finned X-Wing uses two rows and two columns, a Finned Swordfish three of each. The fin rule and the eliminations work the same way, inside the fin's box.

jellyfish.name: Jellyfish
jellyfish.title: Jellyfish in Sudoku: The Four-Line Fish Explained
jellyfish.description: Jellyfish: one digit confined to the same four columns in four rows, or the same four rows in four columns. It is removed from the rest of those lines.
jellyfish.summary: A Jellyfish is the four-line member of the fish family that starts with the [X-Wing](x-wing) and the [Swordfish](swordfish). Pick one digit and four rows in which that digit can only go in the same four columns, each row using two, three or four of them. The four rows need four copies of the digit, one in each row, and those copies can only sit in the four columns, one per column. So the four columns get their copy from these rows, and the digit can be removed from every other cell of the four columns. The same works with rows and columns swapped. The Jellyfish is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When X-Wings and Swordfish find nothing for a digit that still has many candidates spread over the board. Jellyfish are rare, because smaller fish, pairs and other patterns usually solve the digit first, but they do appear in hard puzzles. A full set of notes is needed.
spot: Choose a digit and list, for each row, the columns where it can still go. Look for four rows whose lists together use only four columns; a row may use two, three or four of them, but none may use a column outside the four. Every candidate of the digit in those columns outside the four rows can then be removed. Check columns against rows the same way.

steps: In rows {rows}, digit {d} can only go in columns {cols}: its candidates there are {cells}.
Each of the four rows needs a {d}, and it must be in one of the four columns. Four rows, four columns: the {d}s of these rows take exactly one cell in each of the four columns.
So every column of {cols} gets its {d} from one of rows {rows}.
No other cell of those columns can be {d}. Remove {d} from {elim}.

mistakes: Choosing four rows whose candidates spread over five columns. Every candidate of the digit in the four rows must lie in the same four columns.
Removing the digit from the four rows themselves. The eliminations are in the four columns, outside the four rows.
Missing a smaller fish. If two or three of the rows already form an X-Wing or a Swordfish, use that first: it is simpler to check.
faq: What is a Jellyfish in Sudoku?
A fish pattern of size four: one digit confined to the same four columns in four rows, or to the same four rows in four columns. The digit is removed from the rest of those columns or rows.
How is a Jellyfish related to the X-Wing and the Swordfish?

All three use the same idea with a different number of lines: two for the [X-Wing](x-wing), three for the [Swordfish](swordfish) and four for the Jellyfish. Larger fish are possible, but each one comes with a smaller fish in the other direction, so four lines is the largest size worth looking for.
Does every row need the digit in all four columns?
No. Each row may hold the digit in two, three or four of the columns, as long as no row holds it outside them.
Is the Jellyfish common?
No. Most puzzles that could use one are solved first by smaller fish or other patterns. When the hint names a Jellyfish, the puzzle is usually a hard Expert one.

wxyz-wing.name: WXYZ-Wing
wxyz-wing.title: WXYZ-Wing in Sudoku: How the Technique Works
wxyz-wing.description: WXYZ-Wing: four cells with exactly four candidates between them, bent across two units. The one digit not confined to cells that see each other is removed.
wxyz-wing.summary: A WXYZ-Wing is a wing of four cells that together hold exactly four candidates, W, X, Y and Z, laid out across two crossing units: a row or column and a box, or a row and a column. Three of the digits are confined: each appears only in cells that all see each other, so each can be placed in at most one of the four cells. The fourth digit, Z, appears in cells that do not all see each other. Four cells need four different digits, and the confined digits fill at most three of them, so at least one cell holding Z is Z. Z can therefore be removed from every cell that sees all the cells holding Z. The WXYZ-Wing extends the [XYZ-Wing](xyz-wing) by one cell and one digit, and it is an Expert technique in Bare Sudoku.
when: When the [XYZ-Wing](xyz-wing) and the simpler wings find nothing and the puzzle has a cluster of cells with two to four candidates in one box and the row or column through it. WXYZ-Wings are less common than XYZ-Wings. They need complete notes in the cells involved.
spot: Start from a cell with three or four candidates and collect cells in its box, row or column whose candidates are all among its own, until you have four cells with exactly four candidates between them, lying in two crossing units. For each digit, check whether all the cells holding it see each other. If exactly one digit fails that test, it is Z: every cell outside the four that sees all the cells holding Z loses Z. In the classic form one cell, the pivot, holds all four digits and the other three hold two each, but the pivot may hold fewer, and a wing may hold three.

steps: The four cells {cells} hold exactly four candidates between them: {digits}.
Digits {others} are each confined to cells that see each other, so each of them can occupy at most one of the four cells. Digit {z} is held by {zCells}, which do not all see each other.
The four cells need four different digits. The three confined digits fill at most three cells, so at least one cell is {z}, and it is one of {zCells}.
A cell that sees all of {zCells} can never be {z}. Remove {z} from {elim}.

mistakes: Using four cells with five candidates between them. The count must be exactly four, or the cells could be filled without Z.
Treating a digit as Z when its cells all see each other. Such a digit is confined and can occupy only one cell; Z is the one digit whose cells do not all see each other.
Removing Z from cells that see only some of the cells holding Z. The eliminated cell must see every cell that holds Z, including the pivot if it has Z.
faq: What is a WXYZ-Wing in Sudoku?

Four cells with exactly four candidates between them, bent across two crossing units, in which three digits are each confined to cells that see each other and the fourth, Z, is not. At least one of the cells holding Z is Z, so Z is removed from every cell that sees all of them.
How is a WXYZ-Wing different from an XYZ-Wing?

It has one more cell and one more digit. An XYZ-Wing has a three-candidate pivot and two wings; a WXYZ-Wing usually has a four-candidate pivot and three wings, but it also covers shapes where the digits are shared differently, as long as four cells hold exactly four candidates and only one digit is unconfined.
Does the pivot have to hold all four candidates?
No. Bare Sudoku accepts any four cells with four candidates in two crossing units where exactly one digit is unconfined. The classic pivot with all four digits is simply the most common form.
Is a WXYZ-Wing the same as a bent naked quad?

Yes. A bent naked subset is a naked subset whose cells lie in two crossing units instead of one. When exactly one digit is not confined to cells that see each other, that digit can be removed from cells that see all of its holders. The WXYZ-Wing is the four-cell case; the Y-Wing and the XYZ-Wing are three-cell cases.

bug-plus-1.name: BUG+1
bug-plus-1.title: BUG+1 in Sudoku: The Bivalue Universal Grave Rule
bug-plus-1.description: BUG+1: every unsolved cell has two candidates except one with three. Since the puzzle has one solution, that cell takes the digit seen three times.
bug-plus-1.summary: BUG stands for Bivalue Universal Grave: a position in which every unsolved cell has exactly two candidates and every candidate appears exactly twice in each row, column and box it can still go in. Such a position never has exactly one solution, so a proper puzzle never reaches it. In BUG+1 the board is one candidate away from that grave: every unsolved cell has two candidates except one cell with three, and one of those three digits appears three times in that cell's row, column and box. That digit is the one that keeps the board out of the grave, so the three-candidate cell must be that digit.
